chunks.text: The Cook pine is a tall, narrow conifer endemic to New Caledonia in the South Pacific, where it can reach some 60 metres with a slender, spire-like crown quite distinct from the broader pyramidal shape of its close relative, the Norfolk Island pine, with which it is very often confused in cultivation. Its grey bark peels off in thin papery strips, young foliage is soft and needle-like, and mature foliage becomes small, scale-like and tightly overlapping along the branchlets; female cones are egg-shaped and roughly 10 to 15 centimetres long, while the much smaller male cones look like little foxtails clustered at the branch tips. It owes its common name and scientific recognition to Johann Reinhold Forster, the naturalist aboard Captain James Cook's second Pacific voyage, who first described the species after the expedition observed it on New Caledonia in 1774 — the 'Cook' in the name honours the captain, not the unrelated Cook Islands, a mix-up that persists in casual references. Because of this early confusion with the Norfolk Island pine, a great many potted 'Norfolk pines' sold in mainland nurseries, particularly those raised from Hawaiian seed stock, are in fact Araucaria columnaris. The species' most arresting documented trait, confirmed by a 2017 ecological study, is a geographically consistent lean: trees planted north of the equator tend to tip southward, those south of it tip northward, and those growing almost exactly on the equator stand upright — in every case leaning toward the equator — a pattern whose underlying cause researchers have not fully explained.

This specialist conifer database adds ecological and record-tree detail beyond the general encyclopedic account. In its native New Caledonia the species is strictly a coastal, or littoral, tree: natural stands are rarely found more than about 100 metres from the shoreline, concentrated along the south-eastern and southern coasts of the main island, the Isle of Pines, and several of the Loyalty Islands. Polynesian voyagers are recorded as having deliberately planted it on some of these islands well before Europeans arrived, which complicates any simple reading of which present-day populations are truly wild versus long-ago introduced. The database tracks record-sized individuals grown far from New Caledonia: a tree in Auckland Domain, New Zealand measured at 146 centimetres in trunk diameter and 44.4 metres tall in 2019, and a Hawaiian specimen on Maui measured at over 52 metres in 2025, among the tallest reliably recorded anywhere. It is rated hardy only to roughly USDA zone 10, which explains why it is mainly seen as an ornamental in warm-temperate and subtropical regions such as coastal California, Queensland and the Mediterranean-climate parts of the Americas. The entry also flags that the species' puzzling equatorward lean, formally documented by researchers in 2017, remains an open question in plant biology, with a genetic predisposition toward curved growth suggested as one possible explanation, persisting in the population because it causes no visible disadvantage near the equator where the lean is barely noticeable.
